pass_a_gloss: Last, Antiochus, taking the younger into hands, and having been persuaded that this one too was a brother of those who set such great pains at nothing and had the same choice as those, used other approaches, supposing he would be persuaded by exhortations and by the pledges through oaths about making him wealthy and counted blessed, and having changed from the ancestral things, and being enrolled among friends and being entrusted with royal uses. And as he accomplished nothing at the start, the youth not even attending to the things said, as foreign to his own choice, having called the mother he advised her to become the lad's counsellor for safety. And she, having shown that she would persuade the son about what he wanted, and having jeered at the tyrant, set in motion many words to the son about endurance, so that the youth, not having waited for the punishment being brought on, having anticipated, called forth the public executioners, saying: why do you delay and are slow? for we hear the law given from God; one must not admit an order opposing divine words. But also, as if a king declaring against those judged under him, he declared the judgment against the tyrant, judging him rather than being judged; and he was saying that indeed, having raised hands against the heavenly children, he will not flee the judgment of the all-ruling overseer God.
pass_b_english: Last of all, Antiochus took the youngest into his hands. Convinced that he too was a brother of those who had counted such great pains as nothing, and that he had the same resolve as they did, he tried other approaches. He thought the boy would be won over by appeals and by assurances given on oath that he would make him rich and “envied” if “he turned from the ways of his fathers”, and that he would be enrolled among his Friends and entrusted with royal “offices” (2 Maccabees 7:24).

But when he achieved nothing at all, since the young man paid no attention to what was said, as being foreign to his own resolve, he “called the mother and urged her to become the boy's counsellor for his safety” (2 Maccabees 7:25). She made a show of being about to persuade her son of what the king wanted, and, mocking the tyrant, she stirred her son with many words about endurance, so that the young man did not wait for the punishment that was coming on him but went ahead of it and called out to the executioners: “Why do you delay and hold back? We obey the law given by God; a command that opposes the divine words must not be accepted.”

Indeed, like a king pronouncing on those who are tried before him, he pronounced judgement against the tyrant, judging him rather than being judged; and he declared that, having lifted up his hands against the heavenly children, he would not escape the judgement of God, the Almighty, who sees all (2 Maccabees 7:34-35).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 26); the old English was a digest that replaced Origen's chapter with the mother's speech from 2 Macc 7:27-29 in King James wording ('My son, pity me, who bore thee nine months ...'), which Origen does not quote, and it dropped his own account: the oaths and offers, the mother's show of compliance while mocking the tyrant, the boy calling out to the executioners, and the boy judging the king like a king.

choices.issue: ἄλλαις (M margin) vs ἀλλ᾽ (M text, Wettstein, Delarue)
choices.choice: Koetschau prints ἄλλαις ἐφόδοις: 'he tried other approaches'.
Koetschau supplies καί from 2 Macc 7:24 and writes ἐμπιστευθέντα; translated as printed. 'Friends' capitalised as the court title.

choices.issue: ἐπιδειξαμένη πείσειν (Wettstein and Delarue conjecture ἐπιδεξαμένη 'undertook')
choices.choice: Translated the printed ἐπιδειξαμένη, 'made a show of being about to persuade', which fits the following 'mocking the tyrant'; ἤθελε taken of the king.
Taken as the end of the boy's words (no quotation marks in Koetschau; the narrative is reported speech).
Read ὡς δ᾽, ὡς, ὡς ἄρα, οὐκ.
